newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission president defends work hours law.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission president defends work hours law.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer told British Prime Minister John Major on Tuesday that the European Union's working time law would not shackle business and urged him to implement it as quickly as possible.

"I recall that member states are required to do this by 23 November 1996," Santer said in a letter to Major following a ruling by the European Court of Justice rejecting Britain's challenge to the law.
Santer, responding to a letter from Major about the court ruling, also said the Commission reserved the right to introduce other legislation under the treaty article that Britain contested.

Major said in his letter to Santer and fellow EU leaders that Britain would insist on overturning the law, which sets a maximum average work week of 48 hours, in the Inter-Governmental Conference (IGC) which is considering reforms to the EU treaty.

He said introducing rules that would shackle Britain's flexible labour market was counter to the spirit of the opt-out he won from Social Chapter legislation during negotiations on the Maastricht treaty on economic and political union that took effect in 1993.
But Santer said the Commission had proposed the legislation in 1990, before the Social Chapter existed.

"I have always been of the opinion that adequate social provisions must be part of a well functioning internal market," he said. "In my view, this does not amount to placing unnecessary burdens on businesses or damaging competitiveness."

Britain charged in its court case that the EU had improperly adopted the working time directive as a health and safety measure requiring a majority vote by EU ministers, rather than under more appropriate treaty provisions requiring unanimity.
EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn earlier criticised Britain for "threatening to hold up the IGC for ransom".

"The United Kingdom failed to obtain what it wanted by the front door...They failed by the back door in so far as the court action is concerned," he added. "And now they are attempting to break in through the IGC."
